item.title: Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena and Prolonged Uncertainty
item.description:
Anxiety

Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena and Prolonged Uncertainty

Chronic uncertainty around unexplained phenomena and its psychological effects.

Posted August 23, 2026

Key points
  • Prolonged UAP uncertainty can turn curiosity into powerlessness, anger, and mistrust.
  • Information gaps make false narratives and confident claims more appealing.
  • Honest communication about what is known and unknown can make uncertainty easier to tolerate.
Source: Ahmed/Unsplash

The growing public interest in unidentified anomalous phenomena (UAP) isn’t just about wanting to know what’s in the sky. It is about answering the question of what implications they have for mankind. But as the interest is growing, so is the level of frustration many people are experiencing.

While recent congressional hearings, scientific initiatives, and mainstream media coverage show the previously taboo subject is now being talked about more openly by serious people, the conclusions remain inconclusive.

The PURSUE (Presidential Unsealing and Reporting System for UAP Encounters) files, which Donald Trump specifically stated on his Truth Social account he was releasing so “the people can decide for themselves 'WHAT THE HELL IS GOING ON,'” have received almost 2 billion views. But the information being released is being given without context or explanation and has, thus far, left more questions than answers.

Many government and military officials have gone on record stating they have seen classified information that indicates the possibility of non-human space craft and biologics, but they can’t say more. Even whistleblowers who are trying to provide information, report they can’t give specifics because of NDAs or fear of retaliation.

It always seems as if someone knows something they can’t tell you for some reason.

All of this ambiguity has led to feeling that we may never get the real answers.

And this type of chronic uncertainty has significant psychological implications.

When people feel information is being intentionally withheld, it changes the way they process what’s happening.

Uncertainty Can Become Powerlessness

Humans live with constant uncertainty. We don’t know exactly what will happen in the next five minutes let alone five days, five months, or five years.

But when we start to feel uncertain because it seems like someone else is controlling what we are allowed to know, we stop wondering what’s true and instead begin asking, “Why is the truth being kept from me?”

article continues after advertisement

When you can’t access information you need to answer important questions, you can start to feel powerlessness, which can lead to other negative emotions like suspicion, frustration, and even anger.

Anger can give you a sense of having more power in a situation. It motivates and mobilizes people into action. They may begin to protest or demand answers as a way to help regain control.

But if there is no clear action capable of resolving the uncertainty, that energy has nowhere productive to go. Someone can remain psychologically activated while the situation remains unchanged.

For some people, this may lead to disengagement, they stop caring or paying attention entirely, for others it may cause them to become more proactively involved.

The Search for Closure

When people encounter uncertainty around a subject that has personal meaning they naturally try to soothe their anxiety. In the case of UAPs, they may seek out more information by reading government reports, following congressional hearings, searching historical records, listening to interviews, or becoming actively involved in online communities. Each new document or testimony offers the possibility that they may finally get the missing piece of the puzzle.

But it can also create a cycle of anticipation and disappointment. Every time there is a new hearing, a new witness that comes forward, or a document release is promised, people raise their hopes that this will be confirmation they’ve been looking for, but then definitive evidence never seems to appear.

People can begin to feel deceived or foolish for believing they were finally going to get an answer. And the search for information can start to become emotionally consuming because the brain continues to treat the open question as unfinished business that needs resolving.

Confidence Can Substitute for Evidence

article continues after advertisement

But, when the explanations being given, if there are any at all, are inadequate to explain what we are seeing, let alone answer the ultimate question everyone is asking, which is “are we alone in the universe?” interest doesn't just disappear. People begin to search elsewhere for the answers they need.

Research shows that uncertainty and a lack of control can make people more receptive to false explanations.1 This can open the door to believing in conspiracy theories, particularly those that portray the government as deceptive or threatening.

When no information is being provided, people can begin to mistake voices that seem loud or certain for credibility. A confident explanation feels reassuring, but it does not necessarily mean it is an informed one.

While government communication won’t prevent misinformation, it can reduce the space in which misinformation grows.

The Erosion of Trust

Trust helps people tolerate uncertainty. We do not need all the information ourselves as long as we believe that those who do possess it are competent, honest, and acting in good faith.

Just releasing information does not guarantee trust. Research on government transparency shows it can sometimes reveal disagreement, poor decisions, or uncertainty and may sometimes reduce confidence in the short term.2

But people are more likely to view a process as fair and trustworthy when they believe the government is being transparent, even when they don’t get the outcome they wanted.3 This matters psychologically because fair and understandable procedures make uncertainty easier to tolerate.

article continues after advertisement

People can understand that the government won’t know what every UAP is. But they do want to understand how the evidence is being evaluated, why some information continues to remain classified, what conclusions the available evidence can support, and how open questions are being answered.

Without that understanding, people are left to interpret what the ambiguous information being provided is, as well as what the government’s silence means.

People Can Tolerate Honest Uncertainty

Officials may fear that admitting uncertainty will undermine public confidence, but research suggests that honest uncertainty is often less damaging than expected.

Studies have found that communicating uncertainty does not result in a meaningful reduction in trust in the source providing the information.4 Transparent explanations of the strength and limitations of evidence also don't appear to undermine public trust.5

This kind of communication provides a psychologically important framework.

People can understand that evidence is incomplete or that different explanations are possible. And they can understand that there are good reasons, such as national security, why some information cannot be immediately released. What is harder to tolerate are feelings of ambiguity and uncertainty when there is no clear process for resolving it.

Turning Uncertainty Into a Shared Process

UAP transparency is not dependent on the release of every document, but it does require clear and honest communication that helps people better understand the process as it is unfolding.

Communication, by itself, won’t eliminate uncertainty. But when people understand what's happening, discovering what UAPs are can become a shared scientific problem rather than a process from which they feel excluded.

article continues after advertisement

The search for answers can remain focused on discovering the real evidence rather than driven by a desire to eliminate the discomfort of not knowing.

Whatever the ultimate explanation for UAP may be, the public is already responding psychologically to the process by which information is being investigated and released.

The answers matter, but so does the experience of waiting for them.

item.title: Loving Without Losing Yourself
item.description:
Boundaries

Loving Without Losing Yourself

Ideas about the art of staying whole in a relationship.

Posted August 23, 2026

Key points
  • In all healthy relationships, it's important not to forget your own needs.
  • It's important to maintain boundaries in healthy relatiosnhips.
  • Self-care is important across the life span.

Many people were taught that love means selflessness. But self-erasure does not create strong relationships; it often produces resentment, anxiety, and a relationship in which neither person is fully known and seen.

Losing yourself is not the same as being close to another person. It is an unhealthy fusion in which you give away too much of yourself. This can happen during any stage of life and across generations. For example, many caregivers in the “sandwich generation” are simultaneously supporting children and aging relatives, leaving little room for their own needs. According to Sparrow, 42% of caregivers are part of the sandwich generation, simultaneously caring for both young children and aging relatives.

What Is Loving Without Losing Yourself?

Loving without losing yourself means staying connected to others while remaining loyal to your own truth, body, needs, and voice. Many people have spent decades caring for children, partners, parents, friends, communities, and work. The capacity to love deeply is a strength. Yet when care repeatedly requires us to abandon our needs, silence our truth, or override our limits, love can lead to exhaustion and depletion.

It’s important to remember that if a relationship includes threats, intimidation, coercion, violence, financial control, stalking, or fear for your safety, you should prioritize support and safety instead of confronting the person alone. Reach out to a trusted local advocate, professional, or emergency service as appropriate.

The Importance of Boundaries

Boundaries are important so you don’t fall into exhaustion or depletion. A boundary is not a wall against love. They are a form of self-respect and relationship clarity. Boundaries are a doorway through which honest love can enter.

A boundary can be physical, emotional, time-related, conversational, financial, digital, or practical. For those who are caring and loving, setting boundaries is a practice. A clear boundary is usually brief. Long explanations may invite negotiation. Some would say that “No” is a complete sentence.

Simple Ways to Relay That You Have Boundaries

  • “I’m not available for that.”
  • “I need time to think before I answer.”
  • “That does not work for me.”
  • “I’m willing to talk when we can speak respectfully.”
  • “I won’t be discussing that further.”
  • “I care about you, and I need to take care of myself too.”
  • “I’m going to end this call now. We can try another time.”

Non-Negotiables

A non-negotiable is a condition that protects your well-being, safety, health, values, and time. It is not an attempt to control another person; it simply describes what you will do. Here are some examples of non-negotiables:

  • “I do not continue conversations in which I am yelled at or insulted.”
  • “I need one evening each week with no caregiving or social obligation, except for emergencies.”
  • “I do not lend money I cannot afford to lose.”
  • “I will not discuss private matters with people who repeat them elsewhere.”
article continues after advertisement

What Does Losing Yourself Feel Like?

“Losing yourself” may look quiet: agreeing too quickly, answering every call, keeping a sense of peace but feeling as if it’s costing you. It could also be taking responsibility for someone else’s feelings, while neglecting your own rest and pleasure. Losing yourself can be shaped by family roles, cultural expectations, grief, illness, financial dependence, or a long history of being the reliable one. Many of us were taught that being loving meant being available, agreeable, useful, or self-sacrificing, but this can make stress build up insidiously.

How Stress Builds Up

Feeling stressed does not always have to be dramatic. Sometimes it builds up subtly, quietly, and persistently. You might be productive and getting things done, but your nervous system is under strain. You might be feeling stressed, but thinking "I’ll rest later."

What To Do When You’re Feeling Overwhelmed

  • Reduce stimulation
  • Leave the room and take a five-minute walk without your phone.
  • Sit down and let your shoulders relax before trying to fix anything.
  • Gentle movement can remind your nervous system that you are safe enough to move through the moment.
  • Place a hand over your heart and acknowledge, “I am here. I matter too.”

Reducing Stress Without Avoiding Your Life

  • Some stress requires calming; other stress requires resolution.
  • Create a manageable schedule allowing time for rest.
  • If your mental state is overwhelmed by the constant barrage of negative information, try turning off the television, radio, or social media to decrease stimulation. This helps provide a reset.
  • If you continually find yourself exhausted after interacting with a particular person, it might mean you need to set a boundary.
  • Talk with someone who understands you and can interrupt your cycle of thinking.
  • Journaling is also helpful.
article continues after advertisement

When Guilt Arrives

Guilt is not always a signal that you have done something wrong. Sometimes it’s the discomfort of doing something new—especially if you have a history of putting yourself last. When you feel guilty, try this little exercise:

Pause: Take one slow breath.

Name it: “I am feeling guilt, fear, sadness or pressure.”

Ask: “Have I harmed someone, or am I disappointing an expectation?”

Choose: Return to your values and your limits.

item.title: Understanding Why We Procrastinate
item.description:
Procrastination

Understanding Why We Procrastinate

Not all task avoidance is the same.

Posted August 23, 2026

Key points
  • Procrastination is not laziness or a lack of willpower—it involves a complex set of executive function skills.
  • To overcome procrastination, it is important to understand how this behavior relates to key tasks.
  • Employing key ADHD motivational and calming strategies may help.

Procrastination is a side topic to the key executive function of task initiation. For neurodivergent brains, procrastination is much more complex than it looks. While not starting is often stigmatized as laziness or a lack of willpower, it is actually related to several brain-based skills known as executive functions. Scholars have found that procrastination has various causes that are helpful to be aware of when trying to overcome its presence in our lives.

Reasons We Procrastinate

There are three primary reasons that we often procrastinate. First, sometimes we procrastinate because we aren’t very interested in or motivated by the task or question. In other scenarios, we don’t start because we are too anxious about a task, and that anxiety makes us want to avoid it (this can be experienced consciously or unconsciously). A third scenario is that, other times, the task carries a lot of emotional baggage because it is one we have been chastised for not being able to do or have failed at in the past. In this case, the task has accumulated a lot of self-flagellation or perhaps negative comments from others. This is what Coach Brendan Mahan calls a "wall of awful." When we develop it, it is very difficult to start a task in a scenario where we have a wall of awful—one that has accumulated so much baggage that we dread it and are often immobilized by it.

Overcoming Procrastination

So what do we do when we need to get started on a task? It really depends on the reason why we’re procrastinating in the first place. If the issue really is about a lack of motivation or interest, as Elaine Taylor-Klaus (2020) outlines through the PINCH framework in her book The Essential Guide to Raising Complex Kids with ADHD, Anxiety, and More, it can be helpful to leverage motivators like play, interest, novelty, challenge, or hurry up (deadlines/accountability). In this case, it can be helpful to spend some time thinking about the task and how we could make it more playful, interesting, novel, or challenging, or whether we could add a deadline or some external accountability to the task.

If anxiety is fueling procrastination, then other strategies may be in order. Many of us are driven by anxiety to procrastinate on a task because it is so important to us and we are anxious about it, which leads us to avoid it. If we are anxious about the task, it is important to understand that we may be motivated to avoid it. To overcome avoidance, it will be important to make the task less anxiety-provoking, so we have less desire to avoid it. This may involve making the task smaller or changing the setting in some way so that our urge to avoid is less.

If we have a wall of awful on our hands, we can try some of the strategies above but, if they still don’t work, we may need to try to really understand what’s going on behind our emotional baggage and consider working with a therapist to help us understand how we might be taking the task to be something personal about ourselves, how we might be staying stuck in old failures or how we might be reading failure into similar tasks from the past that are getting in our way.

article continues after advertisement

Conclusion

To conclude, the complex executive function challenge of procrastination has several possible causes. To know which strategies to try, it helps to understand what is fueling the procrastination of a particular task. If you are stuck on a task in a way that is emotionally distressing and feels linked to how you are conceptualizing your identity and worth, you may want to consider working with a therapist on the blockages you’re facing related to a particular kind of important task for you.

To find a therapist, please visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.
